extracted.intended_audience: writers, students, and readers interested in narrative techniques and plot devices
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic overview of plot-twist categories and the mechanics for executing twists in fiction, with definitions, examples, and notes on audience expectations and preparation (foreshadowing, withholding, misdirection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanics of a plot twist
rubrics_metrics.description: A plot twist introduces a radical change in the direction or expected outcome of the plot; it may change the audience's perception of preceding events or introduce a new conflict that places them in a different context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods used to execute a plot twist include foreshadowing (to prepare the audience to accept it), withholding information from the audience, or misleading them with ambiguous or false information. Not every plot has a twist; some have multiple lesser ones and some are defined by a single major twist. Because effectiveness usually relies on the audience not having expected it, revealing a plot twist in advance is commonly regarded as a spoiler.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anagnorisis (discovery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anagnorisis, or discovery, is the protagonist's sudden recognition of their own or another character's true identity or nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reveals previously unforeseen character information. Notable example: Oedipus Rex, where Oedipus learns the truth toward the climax. Early use as a twist ending in a murder mystery occurs in the Arabian Nights tale 'The Three Apples' where discovery of a key item reveals the culprit to have been the investigator's own slave.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flashback (analepsis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Flashback, or analepsis, is a sudden, vivid reversion to a past event that surprises the reader with previously unknown information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A flashback can solve a mystery, place a character in a different light, or reveal the reason for an inexplicable action. Example: Alfred Hitchcock's film Marnie. Sometimes combined with anagnorisis when the flashback reveals a true identity or relation (examples: Once Upon a Time in the West; The Odessa File).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cliffhanger
rubrics_metrics.description: A cliffhanger is a plot device which features a main character in a precarious or difficult dilemma or confronted with a shocking revelation at the end of an episode of serialized fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cliffhangers are intended to incentivize the audience to return to see how the dilemma is resolved. Notable example: The Empire Strikes Back revelation that Darth Vader is Luke's father.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unreliable narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: An unreliable narrator twists the ending by revealing, almost always at the end, that the narrator has manipulated or fabricated the preceding story, forcing the reader to question prior assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often used in noir fiction and films. Examples: The Usual Suspects; Agatha Christie's The Murder of Roger Ackroyd (controversial for perceived unfairness). Can include protagonists revealed to be insane (e.g., Brazil, Fight Club, Shutter Island). The term may also apply to films without conventional voice-over but presented from a protagonist's perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripeteia (reversal of fortune)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peripeteia is a sudden reversal of the protagonist's fortune, whether for good or ill, that emerges naturally from the character's circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must be logical within the frame of the story (unlike deus ex machina). Examples of negative reversal: Agamemnon's murder in The Oresteia; 'Time Enough at Last' (Twilight Zone). Example of positive reversal: The Game.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deus ex machina
rubrics_metrics.description: Deus ex machina refers to an unexpected, artificial or improbable character, device or event introduced suddenly to resolve a situation or untangle a plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originally a literal 'god from the machine' in ancient Greek theatre. Now used pejoratively for contrivances that resolve complications without convincing preparation in preceding action (e.g., discovery of a lost will in Victorian novels). Considered an implausible or unsatisfying way to resolve a plot if not properly prepared/foreshadowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Red herring
rubrics_metrics.description: A red herring is a false clue intended to lead investigators toward an incorrect solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common in detective and mystery fiction as a form of misdirection, distracting protagonist and reader away from correct answers or pertinent clues. Examples: The Da Vinci Code; Primal Fear; Agatha Christie's And Then There Were None. Can function as false foreshadowing. Examples in TV: Lost's second timeline as a red herring.

rubrics_metrics.name: False protagonist
rubrics_metrics.description: A false protagonist is a character presented at the start of the story as the main character but then disposed of, usually killed, to emphasize they will not return.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to shock the audience and subvert expectations. Examples: Psycho's Marion Crane; Drew Barrymore's Casey Becker in Scream; Ned Stark in Game of Thrones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-linear narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: A non-linear narrative works by revealing plot and character in non-chronological order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires the reader to piece together the timeline to fully understand the story. A twist can arise from withholding information until the climax that places characters or events in a different perspective. Early examples: The Odyssey and The Aeneid. Modern examples: Mulholland Drive, Pulp Fiction, Memento, Arrival, Lost, Westworld, Catch-22, WandaVision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse chronology
rubrics_metrics.description: Reverse chronology reveals the plot in reverse order, from final event to initial event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By showing effects before their causes, the initial cause can operate as a 'twist ending.' Examples: Irréversible, Memento, Happy End, 5x2; plays like Betrayal and novels such as Time's Arrow; Merrily We Roll Along uses reverse order on stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spoiler and audience expectation considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Because effectiveness of a twist usually relies on the audience not having expected it, revealing a plot twist to readers or viewers in advance is commonly regarded as a spoiler.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revealing that a work contains twists—especially at the ending—can change audience expectations and be controversial. However, at least one study (cited) suggests revealing spoilers does not necessarily affect enjoyment of a work.
